sections.h2: Installed capacity is about 35% of NIWE's 100m onshore potential

chart.title: Most of Tamil Nadu's assessed onshore wind potential is still unbuilt
chart.sub: Installed capacity against NIWE's 100m potential, MW.
chart.source: NIWE Wind Atlas; MNRE, as cited in the post.

sections.means: Tamil Nadu has built roughly a third of the onshore wind that NIWE assesses at 100m hub height, so most of the resource is still unused.
sections.todo: Repower the oldest sites with taller turbines and close the grid and evacuation gaps that hold back new capacity.

sections.h2: National potential rises from 302 GW to 1,163.9 GW as hub height reaches 150m

chart.title: National assessed wind potential more than triples from 100m to 150m hub height
chart.sub: NIWE assessed national onshore potential by hub height, GW.
chart.source: NIWE atlases, as cited in the post.

sections.means: Taller towers reach faster, steadier wind, so the same corridors become usable at a much larger scale.
sections.todo: Plan repowering and new-build sites against 120m and 150m hub heights rather than the 100m assessment.

sections.h2: Ageing turbines run at 10–15% capacity factor against 25–30% for modern ones

chart.title: Repowering targets 25–30% capacity utilisation against an old fleet's 10–15%
chart.source: Post's own figures on the Tamil Nadu fleet and modern turbines.

sections.means: Most of the gain from repowering comes from taller, larger-rotor turbines on the same land, not from more sites.
sections.todo: Fast-track the state's repowering policy by settling banking-charge, grid-connectivity and evacuation disputes first.

update_notes: Updated 16 November 2026: The Ministry of New and Renewable Energy put Tamil Nadu's installed wind capacity at 12,273 MW on 30 June 2026, second to Gujarat at 16,086 MW, in a PIB release of 22 July 2026. The 11,938 MW and 14,493 MW figures below are for 31 October 2025.
